questions.title: What does the "legislature knows how to" argument mean in statutory interpretation?
questions.question_body: I'm reading this Eighth Circuit opinion interpreting Minnesota's Payment of Wages Act. The court concludes that employees can't seek penalties under § 181.101 because that statute only references the Commissioner regarding penalties. But the court then compares other Minnesota statutes (like § 181.13) that explicitly give employees the right to collect penalties, saying the legislature 'knew how to' give employees that right if it wanted to. Is this a form of expressio unius? Why does the language in a completely different statute tell us anything about legislative intent for this particular statute? This seems like comparing apples to oranges.

questions.title: Can a plaintiff have Article III standing to seek civil penalties payable to the government?
questions.question_body: In this case, Cohen sought statutory penalties under the Minnesota Fair Labor Standards Act. The court notes these penalties are payable to the Commissioner, not to Cohen himself. Yet the court cites Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw for the proposition that civil penalties 'may afford redress to citizen plaintiffs' through deterrence. I'm confused about how a plaintiff has standing to seek penalties that don't go to them personally. I thought standing required a personal injury that the relief would redress. If the penalties go to the government, how do they redress the plaintiff's injury? What's the theory here?

questions.title: Does paying a plaintiff's damages make a claim moot if the challenged policy might still be in effect?
questions.question_body: The defendant in this case paid the plaintiff all overtime wages and liquidated damages he was owed. The parties stipulated he'd been paid everything. But Cohen still sought statutory penalties, and the court remanded to determine if the claim is moot because it's unclear whether Consilio's 'violative overtime policy is still in place.' I'm confused about the mootness analysis here. If Cohen has been fully compensated for his personal losses, why does the ongoing policy matter for his penalties claim? What does 'absolutely clear that the wrongful conduct will not recur' mean in practice? Is this about his standing or about the court's ability to grant meaningful relief?

questions.title: What constitutes 'meaningful argument' to avoid waiver on appeal?
questions.question_body: The court affirmed dismissal of Cohen's MWTA claim because he 'points to no statutory authority allowing for civil penalties' and provided 'no meaningful argument in support of reversal.' The court cites Milligan v. City of Red Oak saying that unsupported assertions waive the issue. But Cohen did bring this claim in his complaint. How much argument is 'enough' on appeal? Does a party need to cite specific cases and statutory text, or is a general reference to the claim sufficient? If the argument was made below, does it still get waived if not adequately briefed on appeal?

questions.title: Can a plaintiff change the injunctive relief they're seeking at summary judgment?
questions.question_body: Cohen's complaint sought specific forms of injunctive relief, but in his summary judgment briefing, he requested different relief—asking the court to order Consilio to rescind its 2019 overtime policy. The court said it 'did not consider it' because the issue wasn't properly before them, citing a rule that 'new claims are properly raised through amended complaints, not opposition briefs.' I'm confused about when a change in requested relief requires an amended complaint versus when it's just a refinement of an existing claim. Isn't summary judgment exactly the time when parties clarify what relief they're asking for? What's the line between refining your claim and creating a new one?

questions.title: Why would an appellate court vacate and remand for the district court to determine jurisdiction instead of deciding it?
questions.question_body: The Eighth Circuit raised a 'serious concern regarding our jurisdiction' on the MFLSA claim, noting potential mootness issues. Instead of deciding whether the claim is moot, the court vacated the summary judgment and remanded for the district court to determine jurisdiction first. Why wouldn't the appellate court just decide the mootness issue itself? If there's a standing or mootness problem, doesn't that mean the plaintiff never properly had a case, or that the court lacks jurisdiction? What's the purpose of sending it back—what facts could the district court develop that would help answer what seems like a legal question?
